title: Root weight bundles and relative coroots over arbitrary rings
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring, $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and $G/S$ a reductive group in [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Let $M$ be a finite-rank free abelian group, and let $T=D_A(M)\hookrightarrow G$ be a closed subgroup [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group, def-weil-closed-immersion] whose geometric fibres are maximal tori. Put $M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z}(M,\mathbf Z)$, and let $\chi_m:T\to\mathbf G_{m,A}$ be the monomial character of $m\in M$. Write $\mathfrak g=\ker(G(A[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))\to G(A))$ for the tangent $A$-module, with addition induced by group multiplication and scalar multiplication induced by $\epsilon\mapsto a\epsilon$. Conjugation by $T$ induces an $A$-linear coaction $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g\otimes_A A[M]$. Put $\mathfrak g_m=\{v:\rho(v)=v\otimes e^m\}$.

The module $\mathfrak g$ is finite projective, meaning a direct summand of a finite free module. The natural inclusion $\operatorname{Lie}(T)\to\mathfrak g$ identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_0$. For every $m\ne0$ and every point $s\in S$, the fibre dimension of $\mathfrak g_m$ is either zero or one. On every geometric fibre the weights with dimension one are exactly the roots of $(G_{\bar s},T_{\bar s})$. The tangent-module comparison with $\operatorname{Lie}(G_B)$ under any ring map $A\to B$ identifies $B\otimes_A\mathfrak g_m$ with its corresponding full-torus weight module. For $B=0$ this comparison is the zero-module identification.

If $\alpha\in M\setminus\{0\}$ has $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ locally free of rank one on all of $S$, there is a group-scheme homomorphism $\alpha^\vee:\mathbf G_{m,A}\to T$ whose geometric fibres are the canonical coroots for $\alpha$ in [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections], namely $t\mapsto v_\alpha(\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1}))$ for the rank-one $\operatorname{SL}_2$ homomorphism, equivalently the unique cocharacter giving its Weyl reflection. Its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. Equivalently, under the monomial classification of homomorphisms of split tori it is a Zariski locally constant function $|S|\to M^\vee$. Roots and weights throughout mean torus characters, not their differentials; no Noetherian, reducedness or connectedness assumption is imposed.

source.place: Introduction to Section 4, printed pp.107-108 (the tangent weight subbundles and zero weight); Lemma 4.1.3, pp.108-109, and Theorem 4.2.6, pp.120-121 (canonical coroot on the rank-one centralizer and arbitrary base change); Definition 5.1.1 and the final localization in Lemma 5.1.3, pp.136-137. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this relative reductive-group structural theorem.

proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$ and let $c:C\to A$ be its identity. An infinitesimal point over the identity is exactly $c+\epsilon d$, with $d$ an $A$-derivation into the $C$-module $A$ defined by $c$: multiplicativity is precisely $d(bb')=c(b)d(b')+c(b')d(b)$. Thus, by the universal property of differentials, $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,A)$ for $P=A\otimes_{C,c}\Omega_{C/A}$. The smooth-affine comparison says that $\Omega_{C/A}$ is finite projective over $C$. Tensor a finite free splitting with $A$ to see that $P$ is a direct summand of a finite free $A$-module; dualizing its inclusion and retraction gives the same property for $\mathfrak g$. Multiplication of infinitesimal group points adds their derivations: in the coproduct, the two terms linear in $\epsilon$ reduce by the two counit identities to $d$ and $d'$. Substitution $\epsilon\mapsto a\epsilon$ multiplies $d$ by $a$. Consequently this identification gives exactly the module operations in the statement.

source.place: Background on Lie functors, printed p.2; Section 4 introduction, printed p.107. Cotangent interpretation expanded by the agent.

proof.text: For $A\to B$, differential base change gives the cotangent module at the identity of $G_B$ as $B\otimes_A P$. The natural map $B\otimes_A P^*\to(B\otimes_A P)^*$ sends $b\otimes f$ to $(b'\otimes p\mapsto bb'f(p))$. It is an isomorphism for finite free $P$, hence for its direct summand $P$ by restricting that isomorphism along the splitting. This proves the tangent-module comparison for every $B$, functorially and compatibly with successive base changes. Differentiate conjugation by the universal point of $T$ over $A[M]$ and use this comparison with $B=A[M]$ to obtain $\rho$. The group action identities give coassociativity and the counit identity. Conjugation is linear on derivations, so $\rho$ is $A$-linear. The same construction over $B$ is the scalar extension of $\rho$. For $B=0$, both cotangent and tangent modules here are zero.

source.place: Background, printed p.2, and Section 4 introduction, p.107: tangent and torus-action base change; explicit direct-summand dual calculation.

proof.text: Choose a basis of $M$ to identify it with $\mathbf Z^r$. Apply the relative torus-bundle weight theorem to the finite projective module of step 1 and the coaction of step 2. It gives $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_m\mathfrak g_m$ with finitely many nonzero finite projective summands, and identifies $B\otimes_A\mathfrak g_m$ with the $m$-summand after every ring map. This summand is also the full-torus weight functor: the coaction equation implies the character equation after evaluating $A[M]\to B'$ at any torus point, and conversely the universal point over $A[M]$ recovers the coaction equation. Thus the comparison is for characters, including in positive characteristic, rather than for their differentials.

source.place: Introduction to Section 4, printed p.107: the M-graded vector bundle and arbitrary base change.

proof.text: At a geometric point $\bar s$ use steps 2-3 to identify the summands with the full-torus weight spaces of $\operatorname{Lie}(G_{\bar s})$. The hypotheses make $G_{\bar s}$ connected reductive and $T_{\bar s}$ maximal. The field rank-one reflection theorem therefore gives its zero space $\operatorname{Lie}(T_{\bar s})$ and one-dimensional nonzero root spaces; the other nonzero characters have zero space. This proves the assertion about geometric roots. For an ordinary $s$, extension of a basis from $\kappa(s)$ to its algebraic closure preserves its length, giving the asserted dimension zero or one over $\kappa(s)$ as well.

source.place: Introduction to Section 4, printed p.107: reduction to geometric fibres and classical root spaces.

proof.text: The inclusion $T\hookrightarrow G$ induces an injective tangent map: the surjection of affine coordinate algebras in the closed-immersion definition makes restriction of derivations injective. As $T$ is commutative its image is in $\mathfrak g_0$. Derivations of its monomials at the identity satisfy $d(e^{m+n})=d(e^m)+d(e^n)$, so $\operatorname{Lie}(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z}(M,A)$, a finite free module. Both this module and $\mathfrak g_0$ are finite projective, and the map is an isomorphism on every geometric fibre by step 4. To conclude over $A$, around each prime trivialize the two projectives. Their ranks there agree, since the fibre map is invertible. Its determinant is outside that prime, so on the further principal open where the determinant is invertible the adjugate matrix supplies an inverse. These opens cover the spectrum. Thus the tangent map identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ with $\mathfrak g_0$ over $A$, even if $A$ is nonreduced.

source.place: Introduction to Section 4, printed p.107: zero weight equality, with the fibre-to-bundle argument written out.

proof.text: Now let $\alpha$ satisfy the root-line hypothesis. In a basis of $M$ apply the relative root rank-one centralizer theorem: if $\alpha=d\alpha_0$ with $\alpha_0$ primitive, put $T_\alpha=\ker\chi_{\alpha_0}$ and $H=C_G(T_\alpha)$. The theorem gives a smooth affine finitely presented closed subgroup, reductive connected geometric fibres with roots exactly $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$, and $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$; the opposite line is locally free of rank one. The torus $T$ remains fibrewise maximal in $H$: any larger torus there would be one in $G$. All these constructions commute with base change. This reduces construction of the coroot to rank one without assuming any globally constant root set for $G$.

Cover $S$ by principal affine opens where the two finite projective root lines are free, using the prime-local-free theorem and intersecting the two neighborhoods. On each open choose a generator $X$ of the positive line. Step 6 verifies every hypothesis of the normalized rank-one Gauss-chart theorem. It supplies $x_+,x_-$ and a homomorphism $h:\mathbf G_m\to T$, characterized by the opposite-root multiplication formula with $1+uv$ invertible. This is a construction on each open; no choice of a global root-line basis is made.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.4, pp.110,116-118, and Theorem 4.2.6, pp.120-121: normalized local Gauss data.

proof.text: Check this $h$ on an algebraically closed fibre $\bar s$. By step 6, $H_{\bar s}$ is the centralizer of $\ker\chi_{\alpha_0}$, a torus of codimension one in $T_{\bar s}$ contained in $\ker\chi_\alpha$ with finite quotient $\ker\chi_\alpha/\ker\chi_{\alpha_0}\cong\mu_d$; so it is the largest subtorus $T_\alpha$ of $\ker\alpha$, and $H_{\bar s}=G_\alpha$ in the field reflection theorem, which makes it reductive of semisimple rank one with maximal torus $T_{\bar s}$. This is the hypothesis of the field rank-one matrix classification, which we now use. Orient the matrix factor so that $\alpha$ is its upper off-diagonal character. The chosen $X$ is $cE_{12}$ with $c\ne0$. The homomorphisms $x_+(u)=1+cuE_{12}$ and $x_-(v)=1+c^{-1}vE_{21}$ (or their projective classes) and $h(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$ (or its class), all with trivial central factor, satisfy the required Gauss chart and identity. Indeed their product has entries $(1,1)=1+uv$, $(1,2)=cu$, $(2,1)=c^{-1}v$, $(2,2)=1$, and its lower-diagonal-upper factorization has diagonal $(1+uv,(1+uv)^{-1})$. Hence uniqueness in the chart theorem identifies them with the triple of step 7. In SL2 the root is $2\chi$ and $h$ is the diagonal cocharacter; in PGL2 the root is the diagonal ratio and that ratio on $h(t)$ is $t^2$; in GL2 the root is $e_1-e_2$ and $h$ is $(1,-1)$. In each case the class of the coordinate swap normalizes the diagonal torus and is not in it, so it is the unique nonidentity element of $N_{G_\alpha}(T)/T$, and it gives $m\mapsto m-\langle m,h\rangle\alpha$, and fixes the central factor. Thus the uniqueness clause of the field reflection theorem identifies $h$ with the canonical coroot. These calculations use no division by the residue characteristic.

source.place: Theorem 4.2.6 proof, printed pp.121-122, comparison with the classical matrix calculation; Example 4.2.5, pp.119-120.

proof.text: On overlaps the homomorphisms $h$ just constructed have the same geometric-fibre coroots by step 8. Split-torus homomorphisms correspond to Zariski locally constant integer matrices, so equality on all geometric fibres forces equality, even over nonreduced bases. Equivalently their local functions with values in $M^\vee$ agree and glue to a locally constant function on $|S|$. The same correspondence produces the global $\alpha^\vee:\mathbf G_{m,A}\to T$. For any $A\to B\ne0$, steps 2-3 and 6 preserve the root-line condition and the centralizer. Each pulled-back triple of step 7 satisfies the same Gauss identities; uniqueness gives the normalized triples over the pulled-back opens. By step 8, their torus factors are the geometric coroots there. The matrix correspondence then identifies their gluing with the pullback of $\alpha^\vee$. This proves arbitrary and successive base-change compatibility. If $B=0$, the source and target are group schemes over the empty scheme and their unique homomorphism is the asserted base change.

source.place: Theorem 4.2.6, pp.120-122 (uniqueness and base change); Section 4.1, p.107 (locally constant characters), and Definition 5.1.1, p.136.

proof_origin.place: Conrad Section 4 introduction, Lemma 4.1.3, Theorems 4.1.4 and 4.2.6; read online, local PDF WANTED. Expanded cotangent/direct-summand and matrix calculations.
